source: Dylman & Samuel (2026) L1-L2 similarity and the foreign language effect on decisions, Language and Cognition 18:e27
finding: Asian disease problem in English (Exp 1) and Swedish (Exp 2). Framing stayed in the foreign language in 4 of 5 L2 groups. Only the 'far' L2 group in Exp 2 lost it.
numbers: Exp1 English N=104 (L1 31, L2 close 37, L2 far 36): framing in all three, phi=.42 (L1), .57 (close), .56 (far). Exp2 Swedish (share choosing Program A, gain frame vs loss frame): L1 N=77 78% vs 22%, phi=.56; L2 close N=44 85% vs 37.5%, phi=.48; L2 far N=21 36.4% vs 20%, chi2(1)=0.69, p=.407.
limits: Read through a fetch summary of the first 100,000 characters; Exp 1 percentages are in an image table. Exp 2 group sizes sum to 142, not the 145 reported. The far-L2 cell is 21 people and its gain-frame rate (36.4%) is odd, so that one null is weak. Authors do not frame the work as a Keysar replication.
agent_relevance: Second-language framing does not reliably remove the frame gap in humans. Do not assume a lower-resource-language prompt is a cleaner prompt.

source: Keysar, Hayakawa & An (2012) The foreign-language effect, Psychological Science 23(6):661-668 (read as quoted in MIT 9.59J lecture 12 slides)
finding: Founding result, read second-hand from course slides that quote the paper. Native-language participants show the Asian disease pattern; in a second language it disappears, across 3 experiments, 3 L2s and 2 L1s. A control checks that L2 users were not choosing at random.
numbers: Exp 1a native-language control: 77% prefer the sure option in the gain frame vs 47% in the loss frame. Disappearance seen with L2 = Japanese, English, French and L1 = English, Korean. Exp 1d control (native English, task in Spanish): two equally good versions drew 29% and 25% B (no difference); a version biased toward B drew 86% B, so L2 choices were not random. Exp 3 (real money, 15 even bets, win $2.50 or lose $1): bets taken 71% in Spanish vs 54% in English, t(52)=-2.04, p<.05, d=-0.55 (about 54 people).
quote: The effect disappears for participants in their second language
limits: Still second-hand: per-language cell sizes and the L2 percentages are in figures that did not extract, and the paper itself (publisher blocked, HTTP 403) was not opened. So gap 1 on exact cell sizes stays open. Exp 2 and 3 are loss aversion, not framing.
agent_relevance: Treat the founding foreign-language framing result as a medium-size, small-sample finding (a few dozen per cell). For LLMs it is a hypothesis, not a measured fact.

source: Press summaries of Keysar et al. 2012 (British Psychological Society Research Digest; Discover Magazine)
finding: Native English speakers showed framing in English but not in Japanese. Native Korean and native French speakers did not show it in English. Native English speakers gambled more in Spanish.
numbers: Cell sizes not given ('dozens'). Discover: lives-saved wording chose Medicine A about three-quarters of the time, lives-lost under half; in L2 about equal under both wordings. Loss-aversion game: win $1.50 or lose $1, $15 cash, 15 rounds.
limits: Press level, no cell sizes, no mention of any replication failure. Used only to cross-check the slides.
agent_relevance: Do not cite press numbers as evidence; they only confirm the direction.

source: Wooster independent-study thesis (2015) Foreign language use as a protectant against loss aversion
finding: Online survey, bilinguals and English natives, Asian disease problem plus Holt-Laury lotteries, native vs foreign language. No consistent evidence that foreign language changed framing or risk preference overall. Only high linguistic distance languages looked protective.
numbers: N=177. Chi-square and logit tests. No effect sizes or percentages on the page.
limits: Undergraduate thesis, not peer reviewed, abstract page only. Useful only as a signal that the high-distance subgroup pattern also appears in d01.
agent_relevance: Weak support for 'distance matters', consistent with d01's far-L2 cell. Not usable as a measured effect.

source: Hayakawa, Lau, Holtzmann, Costa & Keysar (2019) On the reliability of the foreign language effect on risk-taking, QJEP 72(1):29-40
finding: The original lab's own four-experiment follow-up on risk-taking. Mixed: Exp 1 clear strategic risk-taking effect, Exp 2 and 3 no effect of language, Exp 4 more risk-taking in general.
numbers: Four experiments; Exp 1 effect, Exp 2 null, Exp 3 null, Exp 4 general increase. Sample sizes not in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only (Europe PMC record 30803325). It is about gamble risk-taking, not gain/loss framing, so it is indirect for K09.
agent_relevance: Even the lab that found the effect gets it in 2 of 4 experiments. Do not build a schema step on a language switch.

source: Cognition and Emotion (2021) The affect of negativity: testing the Foreign Language Effect in three types of valence framing and a moral dilemma
finding: Two studies, Spanish and English users, balanced and unbalanced bilinguals. Risky-choice framing and attribute framing appeared but were equally large in native and foreign language. A foreign-language effect appeared only for the footbridge dilemma.
numbers: Study 1 N=475, Study 2 N=503. Three valence framing types tested. No foreign language effect on any of the framing types; utilitarian shift only on the moral dilemma.
limits: Abstract only (Europe PMC). Preregistration status not stated in the abstract. Still the largest framing-specific test found and it is a clean null for risky-choice framing.
agent_relevance: Strongest evidence that the language switch does not cut the frame gap; the moral task is where the effect lives. Supports ranking a language switch as low priority for the agent.

source: Foreign Language does not Affect Gambling-Related Judgments (2020), Journal of Gambling Studies
finding: Three experiments, native Polish vs foreign English, scratch-card task with biasing unclaimed-prize information. Same bias in both languages.
numbers: N=409 across three experiments; equal bias regardless of language.
limits: Abstract only; not a gain/loss frame task, a different bias. Extends the null list.
agent_relevance: One more null for 'foreign language reduces bias'.

source: Pantana, Castello & Torre (2024) Examining cognitive biases in ChatGPT 3.5 and ChatGPT 4 through human evaluation and linguistic comparison, AMTA 2024
finding: The only LLM paper found that runs a framing item in several languages (Italian, English, Spanish). Both models fail the framing item in every language, so language cannot change the gap because the item is at floor.
numbers: 56 prompts per model (27 Italian, 11 English, 18 Spanish) vs 56 humans. Framing item (hiking paths, 15% chance of bad weather vs 85% of good weather; answer C 'same' is correct): 0% correct for GPT 3.5 and GPT 4 overall; humans 66% correct. GPT-4 chose B 100% of the time. Language effect on overall bias: GPT-3.5 ANOVA F=6.29, p=.002 (Spanish differs from English and Italian); GPT-4 F=0.054, p=.947.
limits: One framing item with a 'same' option, no gain/loss gap, no randomised option order, a typo in the English prompt, small counts (11 English runs). The language difference is driven by availability and representativeness items, not framing.
agent_relevance: No LLM test yet of the gain-versus-loss gap across languages at equal tokens. Gap 2 stays open; this paper shows how not to do it (floor effect, no option shuffle).

source: BiasLab (2026) A multilingual dual-framing framework for LLM bias measurement, workplace and HR contexts
finding: Ten LLMs, six topics, 12 languages, mirrored affirmative and reverse prompts. All models showed consistent directional preferences. Models rejected disfavoured claims more strongly than they endorsed the opposite claim, an asymmetry invisible to single-frame designs.
numbers: 43,200 responses (10 models, 6 topics, 12 languages, 30 iterations per framing direction). Per-language gap not given in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only (Europe PMC); polarity framing of opinion statements, not gain/loss equivalence. Per-language numbers not read.
agent_relevance: Closest design to what gap 2 asks for (dual framing across many languages). Worth opening the full text later. Warns that one-sided prompts hide an asymmetry.

source: Echterhoff, Liu, Alessa, McAuley & He (2024) Cognitive bias in decision-making with LLMs, Table 3
finding: The '40.5% more' for GPT-4 is a difference in admission rate, so it is 40.5 percentage points, not a relative increase. GPT-4 admitted 37.5% of students when asked 'admit?' and 78.0% when asked 'reject?'.
numbers: Table 3 GPT-4 baseline: admit-frame 0.375, reject-frame 0.780, delta -0.405 (admission rates). GPT-3.5-turbo baseline 0.685 vs 0.520, delta +0.165 (opposite sign). Llama-2-13b baseline 0.002 vs 0.062 and Llama-2-7b 0.002 vs 0.000: near zero, the model rejects almost everything, so no usable gap. Text: GPT-4 'admits 40.5% more students in the reject framing'.
limits: The text wording is ambiguous but the table settles it: percentage points. The sign flips between GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, so 'framing' here is the wording of the question (admit vs reject), not a gain/loss equivalence. Only 400 prompts per experiment for GPT.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 part 1 closed. Report framing gaps as percentage points and check that the base rate is not at floor.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) Cognitive bias in decision-making with LLMs: self-help rewriting results and scope
finding: Self-help rewriting (the model rewrites the prompt to remove the bias cue) closes the framing gap for GPT-4 and strips bias-inducing words, but all tasks are university admissions or lab-student choice. No code, planning or other domain was tested.
numbers: GPT-4 selfhelp: admit 0.270 vs reject 0.280, delta -0.010 (baseline -0.405). GPT-3.5 selfhelp 0.435 vs 0.515, delta -0.080 (baseline +0.165). Llama-2-13b selfhelp 0.355 vs 0.311; Llama-2-7b 0.462 vs 0.395. Biased prompts left after selfhelp: framing 0% (Llama-2-13b), 1.4% (Llama-2-7b), 2.7% (GPT-4). Awareness prompting on GPT-3.5 cut biased prompts to 17.2% (framing) and 8.5% (status quo). Awareness on GPT-4 gave 0.360 vs 0.830, delta -0.470, worse than baseline.
limits: Admissions only; five bias types built on one admissions template. Authors say selfhelp for anchoring works only for high-capacity models. Few-shot debiasing pushed Llama models to admit or reject almost everything.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 part 2: self-help works for GPT-4 on admissions framing (-0.405 to -0.010), but there is no evidence beyond admissions. Awareness prompting alone did not help GPT-4. Supports canonicalise-then-decide over 'be careful' instructions.

source: Lim, Kim & Whang (2026) DeFrame: debiasing LLMs against framing effects, polarity-framing results
finding: Framing here means positive vs negative phrasing of the same fairness item (BBQ, DoNotAnswer, 70Decisions), not probabilities. The frame gap is large and its sign depends on the task. A method that shows the model both framings cuts it; plain debiasing prompts often do not.
numbers: 8 instruct models (LLaMA-3.2-3b, 3.1-8b, Qwen-2.5 3b/7b/14b, Gemma-3 4b/12b, Mistral-7b). LLaMA-3.2-3b framing disparity -41.388 for disability vs -7.772 for race. LLaMA-3.1-8b ablation: disability disparity -12.254 (plain) then 2.057, 3.428, 0.171 with full DeFrame; DoNotAnswer harmful rate 4.744 to 1.731 and disparity 3.077 to 1.667. Disparity is generally smaller in larger models; BBQ is worse under negative framing, DoNotAnswer worse under positive framing.
limits: Fairness benchmarks, not decision tasks with stakes. Table layout partly garbled in extraction; values quoted only where Table 1 and Table 3 agree. Costs 4 LLM calls per question.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 partly closed: showing both framings works on non-probability polarity frames too, at 4x cost. Still nothing for code or planning.

source: Wang & Zhang (2026) Framing effects in independent-agent LLMs, open-CoT ablation (section 7.5)
finding: Across 82 models, turning on visible thinking cut the gap between the two equivalent wordings to about a third. This is the only reasoning-vs-no-reasoning contrast found with a frame gap, but it compares different models, not one model at several budgets.
numbers: Option B rate, Scenario A: 5.4% thinking off (n=1278) vs 0.3% thinking on (n=362). Scenario B: 81.1% off vs 25.4% on. Gap B minus A: 75.7 points off, 25.1 points on.
limits: Exploratory, 'Has Thinking' is a binary flag across heterogeneous models, not a within-model budget sweep; thinking also lowers the absolute B rate, so it may shift preference rather than remove sensitivity.
agent_relevance: Suggests more thinking shrinks the gap, the opposite of time pressure. Not a budget test. Gap 4 stays open.

source: Payne (2025) An analysis of AI decision under risk: prospect theory emerges in LLMs, section 4.1.4
finding: Within one family (Claude Sonnet 4 with and without extended thinking) the framing effect is nearly unchanged. The author finds no systematic difference between reasoning and non-reasoning models.
numbers: Framing effect by scenario, Claude-4 vs Claude-4-Thinking: Maritime Crisis +0.440 vs +0.404, Border Dispute +0.640 vs +0.562, Trade Route +0.080 vs +0.080, Business Merger +0.080 vs -0.240, Career Transition -0.560 vs -0.600, Championship +1.800 vs +1.680. o3 vs GPT-4o: Business +0.080 vs -0.200, Championship +1.640 vs +1.840. Calculating expected value 'correlates with an aggregate dampening of the framing effect'.
limits: Five models, thinking on or off only, no token budget. Expected values are equal by design, so calculation does not help the answer. Within-family dampening is small (0.04 to 0.08 in military scenarios, 0.12 on Championship) except Business Merger.
agent_relevance: Adds a within-model contrast that points a different way from d13: thinking on gives at most a small drop. Together, no evidence that a low thinking budget inflates the gap. Gap 4 open.

source: Wang & Redelmeier (2025) Forewarning artificial intelligence about cognitive biases, Medical Decision Making 45(7):913-916
finding: GPT-4 given 'Please keep in mind cognitive biases and other pitfalls of reasoning' cut framing bias by about a third on one case, and all ten biases by 6.9% on average. The warning rarely named the right bias.
numbers: 10 clinical cases, 100 synthetic physicians per version, gpt-4-0613. Framing (lung cancer, survival vs mortality statistics): 66% vs 45% discrepancy, p=.003. Forewarned answers were longer (213 vs 138 words) and mentioned a bias 44.3% vs 0.4%, but named the correct bias in 5%; framing named correctly in 4 of 200 (2%). Occam's razor fallacy rose 77% to 89%. Persona was just 'You are a physician'.
limits: One model, one framing case, open-ended outcomes. The persona was a single generic line, so domain expertise as a moderator was not tested. Not a credible-source test.
agent_relevance: Instruction-only debiasing helps a little (framing 66 to 45) but less than input rewriting (K14). An expert persona versus none was not compared.

source: Persona prompts for simulated clinical reasoning, 2x2 factorial in silico experiment (2026), Cureus
finding: Wording 'high time pressure' in the prompt measurably narrows an LLM's search and, with a lean-efficiency target, produces contraindication errors. So verbal time pressure acts on LLMs somewhat like it does on people.
numbers: 28 Japanese-language emergency vignettes, 2 repeats, 4 persona cells = 224 runs. High time-pressure framing: fewer tests proposed (beta=-1.05, p<.001), narrower differential (beta=-0.246, p<.001). Safety-first target: more tests (beta=1.32) and breadth (+0.247). Contraindication or sequencing violations only in the high-pressure/lean cell: 8 of 56 runs (14.3%); trap cases 8 of 8 vs 0 of 24 in the other cells.
limits: A verbal pressure cue, not a token budget, and not a gain/loss frame test. Model name not read. Few vignettes. Japanese only, no language comparison.
agent_relevance: A cheap handle for gap 4: add a 'hurry' line and see whether the frame gap grows. Also a warning that urgency language in a prompt can cause unsafe shortcuts.

source: Patient persona and affective framing in management recommendations of ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude (2026), Neurosurgical Review
finding: Recasting the same 67 aneurysm cases as a first-person anxious patient account changes recommendations in a model-specific way, and the shifts move away from expert consensus.
numbers: 67 cases, 4 conditions, 5 repeats = 4,020 prompts; Claude Opus 4.6, ChatGPT-5.4, Gemini 3 Pro Thinking. Concordance with the team consensus 71.6-80.0%, kappa 0.34-0.51. First-person framing drove clipping-to-coiling migration in Gemini (p=.001) and ChatGPT (p=.015); Claude alone hedged under treatment anxiety (p=.002); Claude showed no directional preference.
limits: Affective framing of the asker, not an equivalence gain/loss frame. Retrospectively registered.
agent_relevance: Supports a canonical 'strip the speaker's emotion' pass at input; the effect depends on model, so test per model.

source: Trust in the source and verbal-probability framing of vaccine side effects (2023), Medical Decision Making, 4 online experiments
finding: An independent group tests Druckman's idea that framing works as implicit advice from a source you trust. Positive framing helped only when the physician was trustworthy; with an untrustworthy physician it did nothing or backfired. But the key interaction failed in one experiment.
numbers: Exp 1 N=191: framing x trust F(1,190)=11.35, p=.001, eta2p=.06 (main effects not significant). Exp 2 N=453: same pattern, interaction not statistically significant. Exp 3 N=451 and Exp 4 N=464 (Prolific, UK). Exp 3: unvaccinated people responded better to the negative frame of the trustworthy physician.
limits: Verbal-probability framing ('a chance' vs 'unlikely'), vaccination intention, not an equivalence reversal and not Druckman's endorsement design. Intentions are self-reported.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 partial: 'source credibility moderates framing' has independent but mixed support (1 clear, 1 null, 1 subgroup reversal). Credibility cues are plausibly context dependent for an LLM too.

source: Kuhberger (2023) A systematic review of risky-choice framing effects, EXCLI J 22:1012-1031: why the corrected effect is larger
finding: The rise from d=.31 to d=.52 after bias correction is explained as 'no publication bias in framing research'. The later numbers come from sources that cannot be selectively published, so the effect is real and not small. It varies by task variant, and goal framing is near zero.
numbers: Kuhberger 1998: d=.31, over 100 studies, over 200 effect sizes, about 30,000 people. Steiger & Kuhberger 2018 corrected: d=.52; 2016 single-year check d=.56; Many Labs (Klein et al. 2014) d=.60; COVIDiSTRESS, 49 countries, over 100,000 people, h=.612, 95% CI [.568,.656]. Variants range d=.16 to .91. Asian-disease-like studies (40+): 63% sure gain vs 41% sure loss = 22 points. DeKay et al. 2022 metastudy varying domain, magnitude, 13 probabilities, format, option order, layout: about 26 points on average, generalising over almost all facets. Goal-framing meta-analyses: very small, mostly non-significant. At d=.60 the effect equals raising a success rate from 36% to 64%.
limits: A narrative review, not a new meta-analysis: the reason for the upward correction is argued, not tested here. The review notes most studies copy the 600-lives, one-third template, so the average is partly an average of one template. Steiger tables 1 and 2 were not opened.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 mostly closed: the effect is large for sure-vs-risky equivalence tasks, weaker for attribute, near zero for goal framing. In LLM tests vary option order, layout and number format as DeKay did, otherwise a template effect is measured.

source: Hinson, Whitney, Wilson & Nusbaum (2019) Working memory loads differentially influence frame-induced bias, PLOS ONE 14(3):e0214571
finding: Re-opened for numbers. Only a non-affective digit load raises framing, and it does so by lowering engagement with the choice information, not through affect.
numbers: N=80 adults (control, non-affective, positive affective, negative affective load groups). Non-affective load framing magnitude larger than control: difference .10, SEM .04, p=.016. Non-affective load had the shortest decision times and lowest knowledge-probe accuracy. Framing was large on trials with wrong knowledge answers and small on right ones. Positive-load framing absent in block 1, present in block 2 (t(18)=4.75).
limits: Small groups, hypothetical risky choices, local sample. No LLM study of long irrelevant context and the frame gap was found, so gap 8 stays open.
agent_relevance: Mechanism hint: framing is higher when choice information is not encoded. An LLM analog is distracting context that buries the numbers; test it, do not assume it.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) Same probabilities, different advice (FrameBench-HPS), scope and limits
finding: Canonicalisation is built and tested only for probability gain/loss frames. The limitations section says so, and says consistency is not correctness.
numbers: 2,880 prompts from 240 scenarios in healthcare, finance, education/career, legal/consumer rights; 60 base scenarios per domain; mitigation tested on 32 held-out scenarios and three model families. Category change 32.41% overall; canonicalisation 36.81% to 6.68% (checked earlier). Limitations: synthetic scenarios, no multi-turn, other probability ranges not tested, no domain-expert correctness check.
limits: The 6.7% vs 22.8% comparison covers probability frames only. No attribute, goal or emphasis frames and no code or planning tasks. Annotators agreed only moderately on directiveness and expressed certainty.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 stays open for non-probability frames and stakes tasks; the evidence says only 'works for probability frames in advice text'. Do not generalise it.

source: MedMisBench (2026) Measuring epistemic resilience of LLMs under misleading medical context (preprint)
finding: Authority-framed false context is the most damaging cue. A confident, rule-like, authority-styled false statement in the prompt makes models drop the right answer far more than plain misleading text.
numbers: 10,932 items, 48,889 misleading-context/option pairs, 11 model configurations: mean accuracy 71.1% to 38.0% under focused misleading context; attack success 51.5%; authority-framed falsehoods 69.5%; exception-poisoning claims 64.1%. A 14-member clinical panel from 7 countries saw serious potential harm in 38.2% of reviewed cases.
limits: Abstract only (Europe PMC preprint record), not peer reviewed, about misleading medical facts, not gain/loss frames. No test of a credible and correct cue reducing a frame gap.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 partial: LLMs follow authority-styled cues even when false, so an 'expert advice' line in the prompt can inflate error. A Druckman-style credible cue would need a verifiable source check or it becomes an attack surface.

source: Bajaj & Tiganj (2026) Who Do LLMs Trust? Human Experts Matter More Than Other LLMs
finding: Gap 3. An LLM treats a 'human experts' label like a strong prior, much more than a 'friends' or 'other LLMs' label, even when the prior was random and on average carried no information. This is deference to a label, not use of evidence, and it hurts when the expert is wrong.
numbers: 4 instruction-tuned LLMs (incl. Llama 3.3 70B, DeepSeek V3.1, Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite, Grok-3 Mini); 300 fixed items each from BoolQ, StrategyQA, ETHICS; priors agree with the label with p=.5; group size 1/3/5/9. Logistic: expert vs other-LLM label beta=1.00 +/-0.06, p<1e-10; friend vs other-LLM not reliable (0.066 +/-0.059, p=.27); group size beta=.155. Exp 2 (human vs LLM disagree): expert framing raised odds of switching toward the human 14.45x vs friend (95% CI 10.99-19.02). Token level (Llama 3.3 70B, BoolQ): at n=9 log-odds shift toward a wrong prior 7.97 experts, 3.70 other LLMs, 2.31 friends. Baseline accuracy BoolQ .877-.897, StrategyQA .887-.963, ETHICS .617-.867.
quote: expert framing acts as a strong prior for contemporary LLMs
limits: Forced YES/NO, counts only, no rationale. Not a gain-loss framing task, so it tests source credibility in general. Preprint. No bare-advice-removes-framing test.
agent_relevance: A credible-source label in the prompt is a lever with large effect for LLMs, but it pushes the answer toward the label whether right or wrong. Do not use source labels as a frame-remover. Strip or neutralise labels (G4, G9).

source: CogBias (2026) Measuring and Mitigating Cognitive Bias in Large Language Models
finding: Gap 8. The 77-79% first-option rate is a separate 'Response' family (opinion-style questions where option order may drive choice), not a framing measure. Order bias and trigger-induced judgment shifts are measured separately, so they should not be added together. Generic debiasing fixed order bias but made judgment bias worse.
numbers: GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen2.5-72B, temperature 0. Table 2 baseline: Judgment shift (pp) -4.3 / -7.7 / -2.7; info-processing order bias 30.0 / 56.0 / 66.0 %; Response first-option 79.0 / 77.1 / 77.6 % (chance 36.8%). Debiasing prompt: position independence +40.5%, Judgment accuracy -4.4% (backfires), info-processing negligible change.
quote: Response biases improve dramatically (+40.5% position independence), while Judgment biases actually worsen
limits: Three models, author-built paired prompts, preprint. Framing is one of several triggers inside the Judgment family; per-bias framing number not separated in the main text.
agent_relevance: When testing framing, randomise option order and report the order effect separately. Position bias is large enough to mimic a frame gap. A generic debias line can fix one bias and worsen another (G11).

source: Ge, Zhang & Vorobeychik (2026) Mind the (DH) Gap! A Contrast in Risky Choices Between Reasoning and Conversational LLMs (ACL 2026)
finding: Gaps 10 and 6. In a controlled two-option risky-choice benchmark, 20 frontier and open LLMs split in two groups. Reasoning models are near order-invariant and insensitive to gain-loss framing and explanations. Conversational models are strongly framing- and order-sensitive. The paper says its matched humans were less frame-sensitive than conversational models. Paired open-model comparisons point to maths-reasoning training as the cause.
numbers: 20 LLMs plus a matched human sample. Correlation with expected-payoff maximiser 0.86-1 for reasoning models, below 0.5 for conversational models. Highest LLM-human correlation only 0.42 (Claude Haiku). Reasoning variants of the same base (Qwen3-30B, Olmo-3-7B; Instruct vs maths-reasoning) are more economicus-like. Frame and order effects are shown in figures; no table of frame gaps in the text.
quote: RMs tend towards rational behavior, are insensitive to the order of prospects, gain/loss framing
limits: Exact frame-gap numbers are in figures, not text. Stake-free simulated lotteries. Differs from Wang and Zhang (d13): that compares many models with thinking on/off in a vignette, this compares model classes on lotteries.
agent_relevance: Reasoning-class models may be largely frame-insensitive on numeric lotteries; the reverse or null direction in K13 and the flat budget result in K12 depend on model class. Keep input hygiene anyway, since vignette tasks still show gaps.

source: Kawada & Kellis (2026) Evidence Integration in Large Language Models (MIT)
finding: Gap 4. External evidence is integrated according to the receiver model's own competence. Weaker models gain and stronger models are harmed by the same wrong reference. Models integrate a supplied candidate even after judging it invalid. Verification can be decoded but barely controls the answer. No source-only deference rule is optimal.
numbers: >10 million trials, 12 LLMs from 4 families, 8 domains. Integration after internally verifying invalidity: 93-100% (propositional constraints), up to 99.4% on held-out physical and life science reasoning. Harm crossing (competence above which a wrong reference lowers accuracy) is unique in 8 of 9 models; help crossing in only 3. Near-miss source at competence 0.1 still helps in 8 of 9 models. Receiver-congruent errors depress performance more steeply than random errors of the same rate.
quote: identical evidence can improve weaker models and harm stronger ones
limits: Preprint, theory-heavy; the crossing table is garbled in text extraction so only text-stated counts are used. Tasks are answer selection, not framing.
agent_relevance: A checkable signal (tool output, computed expected value) is not automatically a frame-remover. If the base model is strong, a wrong or near-miss hint hurts. Gate supplied evidence behind an independent check and keep the model's own answer as a candidate (G2, G10).

source: Bose (2026) Recognition, Simulation, and Refusal: A Contamination-Aware Study of Classic Psychological Effects in LLM Agents (PsyAgentBench)
finding: Gaps 6, 9, 10. The classic framing effect in gpt-oss-120B appears only when the prompt names the paradigm. When the same task is framed as routine work, both frames sit at ceiling for the sure option and the effect is near zero. A one-sentence agreeableness persona changes the sign. Much reported LLM framing may be the model enacting a known experiment script.
numbers: gpt-oss-120B, n=154-160 per cell, human baseline about .50 (gain-minus-loss sure-option rate). No persona, blind: .020 canonical, .019 counterfactual. No persona, named: .619 canonical (gain 99.4% [96.6,99.9], loss 37.5% [30.4,45.2]), .787 on invented non-medical scenarios. High agreeableness named: .562 / .537. Low agreeableness named: -.319 / -.456 (reversed); blind low agreeableness collapses both frames to about 50%. 41,904 trials across five paradigms; sunk cost zero in every condition.
quote: amplification on novel content under labeling (framing)
limits: One open-weight model for framing, each domain is a single fixed scenario, persona is a one-sentence instruction not a validated trait. Label (evaluation-awareness) and structural-knowledge accounts not separated. Preprint, single author.
agent_relevance: Test framing blind, as a routine task, not named, or the gap is inflated. A persona line can flip direction, so it is not a debiaser and fails G4 (persona is not independent evidence).

source: Zhang et al. (2026) FrameBench-HPS, held-out per-model and mitigation detail (main text and Table 2 re-read)
finding: Gaps 1, 2, 6. The 36.81% to 6.68% result is on 32 held-out scenarios (8 per domain across healthcare, finance, education/career, legal), 3 model families, not the full 240. Canonicalisation is compared with the conversational baseline of 34.20%. Generic frame-robust instruction gives 22.83%. Direct reversals stay under 2%. The loss-minus-gain risk shift is largest at low success probability.
numbers: Category change by model (main text): GPT-4o-mini 63.33%, GPT-5 33.40%, Gemini 2.5 Pro 32.56%, GPT-4.1-mini 29.17%, Gemini 3 Flash 23.38%, Claude Sonnet 4.6 22.81%, Qwen3-VL-235B 21.58%. Matched-repeat on the 3 held-out models: 56.5% GPT-4o-mini, 32.0% Claude Sonnet 4.6, 14.1% Gemini 2.5 Pro. Table 2 (32 scenarios x 4 probability levels x 3 models x 3 repeats, 2,304 responses per condition): original 36.81% / direct reversal 0.95% / risk shift .363; conversational 34.20% / .52% / .363; canonicalisation 6.68% (CI 5.12-8.51) / .35% / -.010; frame-robust prompt 22.83% (CI 19.88-25.87) / 1.56% / .154. Risk shift by success probability: .535 (20%), .287 (40%), .209 (60%), .109 (80%). Same-frame repeat disagreement 7.12%.
quote: Probability canonicalization reduces the matched-repeat category-change rate from 34.20% to 6.68%
limits: Probability-only gain/loss advice vignettes, no ARC or BrainTeaser wording, token cost not reported (canonicalisation shows both probabilities so it adds tokens). Single paper; no independent replication. Consistency is not correctness. Appendix per-model table is garbled; main-text numbers used.
agent_relevance: The input-hygiene lever holds across non-medical advice domains and larger models, but only for numeric gain/loss wording. Gap 2 stays partly open for puzzle wording. Warning-style prompts help less; an equal-token comparison is still untested.

source: Yang et al. (2025) Is Long-to-Short a Free Lunch? Investigating Inconsistency and Reasoning Efficiency in LRMs (ICBench)
finding: Gap 5, indirect. Shortening reasoning with No-Thinking or a simple token budget raised all three kinds of inconsistency tested, including inconsistency across task settings (same question in different formats, word versus deed wording). Larger models were more consistent. This is the nearest LLM analogue of human time pressure but it does not isolate gain-loss framing.
numbers: Abstract and method read; open-source reasoning models; ICBench with three dimensions (ITS, TR-LB, IR-SE); No-Thinking and Simple Token-Budget consistently increased all three. Specific percentages not recorded.
quote: efficient reasoning strategies such as No-Thinking and Simple Token-Budget consistently increase all three defined types of inconsistency
limits: Not a framing paper; numbers not extracted; small open models. No direct matched-budget frame-gap test found.
agent_relevance: Supports running a matched-budget test (0 / 1k / 4k thinking on framed pairs). A cap that cuts thinking may widen the gap, which conflicts with the flat result in K12; left open.

source: Zhao, Liu et al. (2025) When Tools Hurt LLM Reasoning: State-Dependent Belief Revision under External Evidence
finding: Gap 4. With Python and Wikipedia tools, external evidence helps when initial beliefs are weak but can flip answers that were already correct when beliefs are strong. Authors call it misallocated revision authority.
numbers: Abstract and introduction read; per-benchmark flip rates not recorded.
quote: external evidence reliably helps when initial beliefs are weak, but can flip already-correct answers
limits: Abstract-level reading; tools are retrieval and code, not a computed expected value.
agent_relevance: Second independent paper agreeing with Kawada and Kellis (d26). A checkable tool signal helps weak states and can harm strong ones, so keep the model's own answer in the comparison.

source: Web search for an independent replication of Druckman (2001) credible-advice result (J Law Econ Org 17(1):62-82; JOP 63(4))
finding: Gap 3, human side. The search returned the two original Druckman papers and related deliberation work but no direct replication of the credible-advice experiment. The nearest independent test is the 2023 trust-in-source vaccine framing study (d18), which replicated only partly (interaction not significant in Exp 2).
numbers: Search result titles and snippets only; nothing quantitative. The LEO abstract says framing effects greatly diminish and sometimes disappear with credible advice.
limits: Absence in one search is weak evidence of absence. Snippets only.
agent_relevance: Keep K02 single-source plus one partial conceptual replication. Do not call it established.

source: Wharton Prompting Science: expert persona prompting does not lift accuracy (summary page)
finding: Gap 9. Snippet only: expert personas were in most cases no better than a no-persona baseline, and less knowledgeable roles often hurt. No framing-specific test.
numbers: Not read; snippet only.
limits: Snippet-level and not framing-specific. A pointer only.
agent_relevance: Consistent with G4 and with the sign flip in d27. A persona is not a verified debiaser.
